background.definition: Hemorrhoids are engorged veins in the rectum and anus that generally cause painless bleeding, anal pruritus, and fecal soilage. Internal hemorrhoids occur in the rectum above the dentate line while external hemorrhoids occur below and contain somatic pain receptors. Complications of hemorrhoids include prolapse, thrombosis, and strangulation.

Incidence is similar in men and women.
Uncommon in those younger than 20.
Common in pregnancy, especially the third trimester and after delivery.
40 per 1000 persons in the general population.

Obesity

Adequate dietary intake of water and fiber to avoid hard stools and early treatment of constipation. C
Eliminate straining during defecation and minimize bowel movement time. C
Advise patients to stay physically active and avoid long periods of sitting. C
Higher risk patients with rectal bleeding () warrant further evaluation with colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy combined with barium enema. C
The duration and severity of rectal bleeding, as well as history of fiber intake and bowel habits, are essential components of the initial evaluation for hemorrhoids. C
Classify internal hemorrhoids as grade 1, grade 2, grade 3, or grade 4 to direct appropriate treatment (). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Linear mucosal tear on examination; markedly increased sphincter tone and sharp, tearing pain on digital rectal examination
Anal pain, anal itching and soreness of skin adjacent to anal margin
Small draining perianal tract; associated with Crohn’s disease
Tenderness, swelling and pain; sometimes associated with fever or chills
Localized infection of an anal gland; pus visible on anoscopy at the dentate line

list.listitem: Take a history of the duration, severity, and exact nature of the patient’s symptoms, dietary history, as well as specific information about frequency of defecation, history of straining and constipation, bowel movement time, wiping, and fecal soiling. Obtain a targeted past medical history and family medical history looking for risk factors for colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, and/or other forms of colitis.
Perform visual inspection, anoscopy, and digital rectal examination in symptomatic patients.
Anoscopy is indicated to confirm or exclude diagnosis or internal hemorrhoids.

Hemorrhoids are soft, often reddish purple, cystic or sac-like structures palpable on external or digital rectal examination. Thrombosed hemorrhoids are firm, smooth, engorged veins that appear inflamed and are exquisitely tender to palpation.

The dentate or pectinate line is the transition from skin (squamous epithelium) to mucosa (columnar epithelium) in the rectum and can be identified visually as an irregular line with the superior mucosal lining appearing more pink and glistening. Rectal masses are more classically firm, irregular, solid structures that require further investigation. Classify the grade of hemorrhoids to guide subsequent therapy ().

Patients most often will complain of painless rectal bleeding, fecal soilage, and/or itching with defecation. Small amounts of bright red blood on toilet paper after wiping or larger amounts of bright red blood in the toilet bowl are typical.
Discomfort and a small, palpable lump during defecation is indicative of a prolapsing internal hemorrhoid or thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
The presence of perianal skin tags supports a prior history of external hemorrhoids.
Fever, draining pus, and dark red blood or melena are not consistent with hemorrhoids and other causes should be evaluated.
Irritation and burning when cleaning the perianal skin is a common complication.
Proctoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy can be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Higher risk patients () warrant further evaluation with colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy combined with barium enema. In one case series of 290 consecutive patients with hemorrhoids and bleeding, over half had coincidental pathology (eg, diverticula, polyps, cancer, angiodysplasia and varices or colitis).
If internal hemorrhoids are identified, classify them according to severity ().
Evaluate thrombosed external hemorrhoids presenting within 72 hours of onset for possible surgical excision. After 72 hours, surgical excision is not beneficial.
Higher risk patients () warrant further evaluation to rule out malignancy.
Medical management with topical steroids and analgesics is appropriate for symptomatic external hemorrhoids and grade 1 internal hemorrhoids. Combination preparations simplify treatment. C
Fiber supplementation (psylliumpowder, 20-30 g per day) helps relieve overall symptoms of bleeding inpatients with symptomatic hemorrhoids. B

Nonoperative techniques including sclerotherapy, infrared coagulation, bipolar probe coagulation, and banding are most appropriate for grade 2 and grade 3 hemorrhoids or grade 1 lesions that fail medical treatment. C

Excisional hemorrhoidectomy results in higher remission rates compared with rubber band ligation for grade 3 hemorrhoids but with increased pain, a higher complication rate, and more time away from work. B

Stapled hemorrhoidopexy, while less painful and associated with a quicker recovery rate, has a higher risk of hemorrhoid recurrence compared with traditional excisional hemorrhoidectomy; the LigaSure procedure may offer a better alternative with less recurrence. B
Transanal hemorrhoidal dearterialization is less invasive has similar results to stapled hemorrhoidopexy, other than a slightly higher risk of recurrence., B

Medical management with topical steroids and analgesics is most appropriate for symptomatic external hemorrhoids and grade 1 internal hemorrhoids. Combination preparations simplify treatment. Avoid long-term use of topical steroids.
For thrombosed external hemorrhoids, nitrogylcerin 0.2% ointment and nifedipine 0.3% ointment may reduce pain.

RCTs have found efficacy for short-term pain relief after hemorrhoidectomy with 10% topical metronidazole, sucralfate, nitroglycerin, and EMLA cream. Larger trials with head-to-head comparisons and combination strategies are needed.
Indications for surgery are shown in .

Multiple RCTs evaluating sclerotherapy, infrared coagulation, and bipolar current treatment modalities have identified no clear advantage of one treatment approach over another for grade 1, grade 2, and grade 3 hemorrhoids. Each is associated with higher complication and recurrent rates than rubber band ligation, particularly for grade 2 lesions.

A systematic review identified 26 studies with 3137 participants among patients with grade III or IV hemorrhoids. This was a network meta-analysis comparing 14 different surgical approaches. They arrived at a number of conclusions: 1) 10 less pain with laser, IR photocoagulation and stapling than with open or closed hemorrhoidecotmy; 2) fewer post-op complications with IR photocoagulation and LigaSure compared to suture ligation and open hemorrhoidectomy; and 3) faster return to work with Doppler guided and stapled approaches than with laser or open hemorrhoidectomy.
There is limited evidence on the utility of botulinum toxin to reduce post-operative pain after hemorrhoidectomy.

A Cochrane review of 3 poor-quality studies concluded that grade 2 hemorrhoids are best treated with rubber band ligation. Excisional hemorrhoidectomy results in higher remission rates compared with rubber band ligation for grade 3 hemorrhoids but with increased pain, a higher complication rate, and more time away from work. Patient acceptance of both treatments is similar, implying that long-term cure may be more important to patients than minor complications.

A systematic review identified 8 studies that while rubber band ligation was associated with fewer complications and less pain post-op, symptom control was better with hemorrhoidectomy. Patient satisfaction was similar.
Bupivacaine injection after hemorrhoidal banding provides modest pain relief 30 minutes after the procedure, but no difference in pain scores at 6, 24, and 48 hours.
Hemorrhoidal artery ligation leads to less recurrence than rubber band ligation but is more painful.

A single RCT found that less invasive sclerotherapy of grade 3 and grade 4 internal hemorrhoids with a proprietary agent resulted in a shorter hospital stay but a 16% 1-year recurrence rate compared with 2% for traditional hemorrhoidectomy surgery.
Endoscopic injection of ALTA (aluminum potassium sulfate and tannic acid) led to cure or improvement in 97% of patients with recurrence in 10% of patients.

A Cochrane systematic review found that SH has a higher risk of hemorrhoid recurrence (OR = 3.22; 95% CI, 1.59-6.51), prolapse (OR = 2.65; 95% CI, 1.45-4.85) and additional operative procedures (OR = 2.75; 95% CI, 1.31-5.77) compared with traditional excisional hemorrhoidectomy. Recurrence and prolapse rates were higher in studies with follow-up of 1 year or more (OR = 3.6 and 3.14, respectively).

A systematic review of 12 studies found faster return to work and less pain with equal efficacy with use of the proprietary LigaSure hemostasis system compared with conventional diathermy. One RCT found comparable outcomes between LigaSure and stapled hemorrhoidopexy, with a lower rate of residual prolapse for the LigaSure procedure at both 4 weeks (5.9% vs 23.5%) and 1 year (2.9% vs 11.8%).

Multiple small studies evaluating the role of internal sphincterotomy in combination with excisional hemorrhoidectomy have shown mixed results. Anal canal pressures are reduced from preprocedure levels but the procedure appears to increase fecal incontinence rates. Sphincterotomy is not appropriate for patients with normal resting anal pressures.

A meta-analysis limited by significant statistical heterogeneity concluded that open and closed techniques for hemorrhoidectomy are equally effective and safe. Faster wound healing was observed with the closed technique.

Transanal hemorrhoidal dearterialization (THD) has emerged as a less invasive alternative. In one systematic review, authors reported low quality studies with just under 2,000 patients; hospital stay was one day, return to normal activities averaged 2-3 days, major bleeding occurred in three patients, recurrence rate at one or more years was 10.8% for prolapse, 9.7% for bleeding, and 8.7% for pain at defecation with increased recurrence for grade 4 hemorrhoids (range: 11.1%-59.3%). Additional high-quality research is needed.

A systematic review identified 8 RCTs with 977 patients comparing stapled hemorrhoidopexy (SH) with transanal hemorrhoidal dearterialization (THD). There were no significant differences between groups with regards to long-term recurrence, pain, hospital time, or return to work. A second systematic review published at the same time that was more selective in study inclusion (6 RCTs with 554 patients) found similar results between SH and THD other than a higher likelihood of recurrence or persistence of symptoms in the THD group (13.2% vs 6.9%).

A systematic review reported pooled bleeding rates of 0% to 2% for laser hemorrhoidectomy (LH) and 5% to 17% for hemorrhoidal laser procedure (HeLP). Symptoms resolution ranged from 70% to 100% for LH and 84% to 90% for HeLP.

Butcher’s broom (Ruscus aculeatus) was shown in one report to reduce pain and overall severity of symptoms after 7 days of treatment. Patients took six 150-mg capsules per day for 3 days and then four capsules per day.

Limited evidence has demonstrated that horse chestnut (aescin extract fromAesculus hippocastanum) taken in 40-mg capsules three times a day for 2 months can reduce pain, bleeding, and swelling associated with acute hemorrhoids. It is also available in a 2% cream. It should not be used in patients with liver or kidney disease.

A Cochrane review of 9 trials of Chinese medicinal herbs found weak evidence to support alleviation of some hemorrhoidal symptoms with some herbal formulae (eg, Radix Sanguisorbae, Radix Rehmanniae, Fructus Sophorae, Radix Angelicae Sinensis, Radix Scutellariae).
A French maritime pine bark extract Pycnogenol (in both oral and topical form) was found in one placebo controlled RCT to improve hemorrhoidal symptoms and bleeding.

The popular astringent witch hazel is commonly used for acute relief of hemorrhoidal symptoms but clinical trial evidence is lacking. Similarly, aloe, catechin, rose hips, and other substances containing flavonoids are often recommended but evidence of efficacy is lacking.

A Cochrane reviewed showed a heterogeneous class of medications and herbals, phlebotonics, improves itching and bleeding and overall symptoms. The phlebotonics include flavonoid plant extracts and calcium dobesilate.

Meta-analysis of seven RCTs of moderate quality with 378 patients found fiber supplements (psyllium, sterculia, and unprocessed bran) to be beneficial in relieving overall symptoms and bleeding in patients with symptomatic hemorrhoids. Increased dietary intake of fiber was not studied. Incidence of prolapsing was not improved with fiber.
Based on a limited systematic review of low-quality studies, sitz baths do not appear to add any value to the treatment of anorectal disorders.
Spicy foods, at least red hot chili peppers, do not exacerbate hemorrhoidal symptoms in patients with second- and third-degree hemorrhoids.
Three RCTs of micronized, purified flavonoids from citrus fruits showed that they helped to control rectal bleeding in grade 1 to grade 2 hemorrhoids.
Refer for nonsurgical interventions based on personal skill level and local availability of treatment options.
For surgical evaluation, refer to a colorectal surgeon.
Clinical evidence of necrotic tissue or concern for a strangulated hemorrhoid requires hospital admission and urgent surgical evaluation.

Observation and pain control for acute thrombosis of hemorrhoids is a reasonable treatment approach. Office-based excision and surgical intervention are alternate treatment options for patients presenting within 48 to 72 hours of thrombosis.

An RCT evaluated a modified approach to the Longo staple hemorrhoidopexy used in elective procedures to treat acute internal thrombosed hemorrhoids. Short-term benefits for patients were seen compared with excisional hemorrhoidectomy, and long-term patient satisfaction was equal but limited to 12 weeks.

Authors of a systematic review of pain management after surgical hemorrhoidectomy recommend local anaesthetic infiltration, either as a sole technique or as an adjunct to general or regional anesthesia, and analgesic combinations (NSAIDs, paracetamol and opiates).

A systematic review found that while very rare, sepsis can occur after treatment of hemorrhoids, often resulting insignificant morbidity including death. Case reports of sepsis following rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, cryotherapy, and excisional and stapled hemorrhoidopexy procedures have been identified.
Most painful hemorrhoids will resolve without treatment in 1 to 2 weeks; even thrombosed hemorrhoids will usually resolve without treatment in 7 to 10 days. C
Grade 2, grade 3, and grade 4 hemorrhoids are less likely to resolve on their own and often require either nonsurgical or surgical intervention. C

Monitor patients undergoing hemorrhoidectomy closely for complications including urinary retention, infection, fecal impaction, and delayed hemorrhage. Anticipate significant universal postprocedure pain. C

Hemorrhoids are common during pregnancy and the puerperium. A Cochrane review of two small studies with 150 women found thatoral derivatives of the flavonoid rutin reduced hemorrhoid symptoms reported by women. Routine use cannot be recommended until safety concerns are further evaluated. The use of dietary measures, fiber, and common topical therapies have not been systematically evaluated in this population but are often recommended.
